claim: Neurons in primary visual cortex (V1) are selective for the orientation of visual contours.
source: The encoding of contour orientation in the visual system begins in primary visual cortex (V1) with neurons selective for the orientation of visual contours
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Blasdel and Salama, 1986; Grinvald et al., 1986)

claim: V2 contains neurons selective for cue-invariant contour orientation.
source: in the second visual area (V2), with neurons selective for cue-invariant contour orientation (that is, independent of whether contours are defined by luminance, motion, color, or depth cues)
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Ramsden et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2016)

claim: Orientation domains exist in V1.
source: These two functions are first embodied in the 'orientation domain' in V1 (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Blasdel and Salama, 1986; Grinvald et al., 1986)
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: Higher order orientation domains exist in V2.
source: the 'higher order orientation domain' in V2 (Ramsden et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: V4 neurons are responsive to contour curvature.
source: V4 neurons are responsive to contour curvature and can be selective for degree of curvature and orientation of curvature (Pasupathy and Connor, 2001; Nandy et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: V4 neurons can be selective for degree of curvature and orientation of curvature.
source: V4 neurons are responsive to contour curvature and can be selective for degree of curvature and orientation of curvature (Pasupathy and Connor, 2001; Nandy et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: It is unknown whether neuronal responses to curvature in V4 are organized in any way akin to orientation maps in V1 and V2.
source: However, it is unknown whether such neuronal responses are organized in any way akin to orientation maps in V1 and V2.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the literature

claim: V4 comprises alternating bands of 'orientation' and 'color' preference.
source: Previous studies have shown the functional organization of V4 comprises alternating bands of 'orientation' and 'color' preference (Tanigawa et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013; Ghose and Ts'o, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: V4 contains organization for disparity defined orientation.
source: as well as organization for disparity defined orientation (Fang et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: V4 contains organization for motion direction.
source: motion direction (Li et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: V4 contains organization for spatial frequency.
source: and spatial frequency (Lu et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Maps for curvature organization have not been demonstrated in V4.
source: but maps for curvature organization have not been demonstrated
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap

claim: Orientation bands in V4 are regions of shape representation that include both orientation and curvature domains.
source: Here, we hypothesized that orientation bands in V4 are regions of shape representation that include both orientation and curvature domains.
evidence: Stated hypothesis of the study

claim: Curvature domains exist in V4 of macaque monkey.
source: Using intrinsic signal optical imaging in Macaque area V4, we find sub-millimeter sized modules for curvature representation
evidence: Supported by experimental data from intrinsic signal optical imaging

claim: Curvature domains in V4 are sub-millimeter sized modules.
source: Using intrinsic signal optical imaging in Macaque area V4, we find sub-millimeter sized modules for curvature representation
evidence: Supported by experimental data from intrinsic signal optical imaging

claim: Curvature domains in V4 are organized from low to high curvatures.
source: we find sub-millimeter sized modules for curvature representation that are organized from low to high curvatures
evidence: Supported by experimental data from intrinsic signal optical imaging

claim: V4 contains domains with complex curvature preference.
source: as well as domains with complex curvature preference
evidence: Supported by experimental data from intrinsic signal optical imaging

claim: A possible 'curvature hypercolumn' exists within V4.
source: We propose a possible 'curvature hypercolumn' within V4.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings

claim: Key emergent functions at each stage of cortical processing are represented in systematic, modular maps.
source: In combination with previous studies, we suggest that the key emergent functions at each stage of cortical processing are represented in systematic, modular maps.
evidence: Inference from current data combined with previous studies

claim: Data was acquired from three hemispheres of two adult macaque monkeys.
source: Data was acquired from three hemispheres of two adult macaque monkeys (one male and one female, Macaca mulatta).
evidence: Experimental methods description

claim: Alternating regions (bands) of color preference vs. orientation preference were observed in V4.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Tanigawa et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013; Ghose and Ts'o, 2017), alternating regions (bands) of color preference vs. orientation preference were observed in V4
evidence: Experimental observation consistent with cited literature

claim: Curvature domains were distinct from color domains in V4.
source: We found that curvature domains (Figure 2G–I, red pixels) were distinct from color domains (Figure 2G, green pixels)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-I

claim: Curvature domains were distinct from high spatial frequency domains in V4.
source: they were also distinct from high spatial frequency domains (Figure 2H, green pixels)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H

claim: Curvature responses are not simply due to the high spatial frequency components of the curved grating.
source: they were also distinct from high spatial frequency domains (Figure 2H, green pixels), suggesting that these curvature responses are not simply due to the high spatial frequency components of the curved grating
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing spatial distinctness

claim: Curvature domains fell largely within the orientation band in V4.
source: As predicted, the curvature domains fell largely within the orientation band and were in close proximity to the straight orientation domains (Figure 2I, green pixels).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I

claim: There is limited overlap between color and curvature domains (5.7% overlap across all three cases).
source: there is limited overlap between color and curvature domains (overlay in Figure 2G, Case 1, 4.9% overlap; all three cases, 5.7% overlap)
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data

claim: There is 13.9% overlap between high spatial frequency and curvature domains across all three cases.
source: and between high spatial frequency and curvature domains (overlay in Figure 2H, Case 1, 26.1% overlap; all three cases, 13.9% overlap)
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data

claim: There is 43.0% overlap between curvature and orientation domains across all three cases.
source: However, there is much greater overlap between curvature and orientation domains (Figure 2I, Case 1, 54.9% overlap; all three cases, 43.0% overlap)
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data

claim: Curvature and orientation domains may be different components of a shape information processing architecture.
source: raising the possibility that curvature and orientation domains are different components of a shape information processing architecture
evidence: Inference from overlap data

claim: Curvature domains appear distinct from orientation domains and have a semi-regular distribution within the orientation band.
source: When overlaid on outlines of orientation domains, curvature domains appear distinct from orientation domains, and have a semi-regular distribution within the orientation band (Figure 2F, color: iso-orientation contours, gray patches: curvature domains).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: The sizes of curvature domains (mean = 434 μm for all three cases) fall within the 200–500 μm range of functional domain sizes in V4.
source: In addition, the sizes of curvature domains (mean = 434 μm for all three cases) fall within the 200–500 μm range of functional domain sizes in V4 (Tanigawa et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013; Ghose and Ts'o, 2017).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data compared with cited literature

claim: Curvature maps are not artifactual.
source: These data thus suggest that curvature maps are not artifactual and are distinct from previously described functional maps in V4.
evidence: Inference from multiple lines of experimental evidence

claim: Color domains exhibited robust response to isoluminant color gratings but weak response to achromatic gratings.
source: As expected (Figure 2L, Col), color domains exhibited robust response to isoluminant color gratings (black) but weak response to achromatic gratings (gray)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L

claim: Color domains failed to distinguish curved vs straight gratings.
source: and failed to distinguished curved (red) vs straight (gray) gratings (Wilcoxon test, p=0.06, all three cases)
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: High spatial frequency preference domains responded strongly to achromatic gratings of high spatial frequency but poorly to low spatial frequency gratings.
source: Similarly (Figure 2L, HSF), high spatial frequency preference domains responded strongly to achromatic gratings of high spatial frequency (black) but poorly to low spatial frequency gratings (gray)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L

claim: High spatial frequency domains failed to distinguish curved vs. straight gratings.
source: and failed to distinguish curved (red) vs. straight (gray) gratings (high spatial frequency domains, p=0.77, all three cases)
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Curvature processing is not subserved by color or high spatial frequency domains.
source: These analyses indicate that curvature processing is not subserved by color or high spatial frequency domains.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: Straight orientation domains exhibited strongest response to gratings of their respective optimal orientations, weak responses to other straight orientations, and weak response to curved gratings.
source: As expected (Figure 2L, 0°, 45°, 90°, 135°), straight orientation domains exhibited strongest response to gratings of their respective optimal orientations (black), weak responses to other straight orientations (gray), and weak response to curved gratings (red).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L

claim: Curvature domains exhibited strong preference for curvature stimuli.
source: Curvature domains, in contrast, exhibited strong preference for curvature stimuli.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Curvature domains displayed preference for curved over straight contours for both grating and line stimuli.
source: Thus, curvature domains displayed preference for curved over straight contours for both grating and line stimuli, supporting a curvature-specific response.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from multiple stimulus types

claim: Curvature domains are strongly selective for curvature stimuli.
source: These data show that (1) curvature domains are strongly selective for curvature stimuli
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Non-curvature domains exhibit minimal response to curvature stimuli.
source: and (2) non-curvature domains exhibit minimal response to curvature stimuli
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Curvature domains in V4 exhibit response preferences that are selective for curvature and are maintained across two types of curvature stimulus (gratings and lines).
source: Thus, curvature domains in V4 exhibit response preferences that are selective for curvature (compared to straight, color, high spatial frequency) and are maintained across two types of curvature stimulus (gratings and lines).
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Curvature preferring domains were not observed in V1.
source: These curvature preferring domains were not observed in V1 (one case shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 10), consistent with previous studies (Yue et al., 2014; Ponce et al., 2017).
evidence: Experimental observation consistent with cited literature

claim: Higher correlation values tended to occur between curvature maps of similar curvature degree.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, higher correlation values tended to occur between curvature maps of similar curvature degree (orange and yellow squares in upper left quadrant and lower right quadrant)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: Lower correlation values occurred between curvature maps of dissimilar curvature degree.
source: and lower correlation values between those of dissimilar curvature degree (green and blue squares in upper left quadrant and lower right quadrant)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: The lowest correlation values were obtained between opposing curvatures.
source: Within this correlation matrix, the lowest correlation values were obtained between opposing curvatures (upper right quadrant and lower left quadrant)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis

claim: Low correlation values were obtained between curved and straight stimuli.
source: and between curved and straight stimuli (rightmost column)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis

claim: Correlation values dropped off with increasing differences in degree of curvature.
source: correlation values dropped off with increasing differences in degree of curvature (green and blue boxes) (e.g. 2–3, 2–4, 2–5)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis

claim: There is a declining correlation with curvature difference.
source: This declining correlation with curvature difference suggests the presence of a shifting map of curvature degree.
evidence: Inference from correlation analysis

claim: High correlation values occur only between curvature gratings of the same orientation.
source: These correlation values illustrate that high correlation values (orange, yellow) occur only between curvature gratings of the same orientation (e.g. 1–5, 2–6)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Low correlation values occur between curvatures of different orientations.
source: and low correlation values occur between curvatures of different orientations (green boxes in columns 1–8, e.g. 1–2, 3–4)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Low correlation values occur between curved and straight gratings.
source: The finding that the low correlation values occur between these curved and straight gratings (columns 9–12) supports the distinctness of straight vs. curved contour representation.
evidence: Inference from correlation analysis

claim: Curvature domains contain subregions of high curvature preference.
source: Figure 5 shows that curvature domains (Figure 5A, Case one and Case 2, white pixels: curvature vs. straight) contain subregions of high curvature preference (red pixels: high curvature vs. low curvature).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: High curvature subdomains prefer high curvature over low curvature.
source: This is shown by preference (Figure 5B, Case 1) for high (dark red lines) over low (light red lines) curvature and even weaker response to straight gratings (gray lines).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Curvature subdomains exhibit graded response to curvature degree.
source: Moreover, the response magnitudes of these subregions gradually diminish with curvature degree difference (Figure 5C, dark to light lines plot responses of high to low curvature; left: upwards curvature, right: downwards curvature).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Paired opposing curvature orientations occupy roughly complementary positions within the curvature domains.
source: Figure 6 illustrates the finding that paired opposing curvature orientations occupy roughly complementary positions within the curvature domains.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: Pixels that prefer upwards curvature maintain their preference across curved gratings and two degrees of curved lines.
source: Figure 6B,C show that pixels that prefer upwards maintain their preference across curved gratings (6B) and two degrees of curved lines (6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C

claim: Pixels that prefer downwards curvature maintain their preference across curved gratings and two degrees of curved lines.
source: This is also true for downwards pixels (6B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C

claim: The average percentage of pixels responsive to two opposite orientations within curvature domains was 22.4%.
source: Within the curvature domains, the average percentage of pixels responsive to two opposite orientations (overlapped pixels vs. all colored pixels) was 22.4% (Case 1: 32.1%; Case 2: 14.9%; Case 3: 20.3%).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data

claim: There are spatial progressions from straight to curved domains in V4.
source: We observed a spatial progression from the center of the straight orientation domain (blue dot in center of blue dotted line) to low curvature domain (blue-oranges) to high curvature domain (orange)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7

claim: Progressions arising from a single orientation domain can lead to two different curvature domains.
source: Progressions arising from a single orientation domain can lead to two different curvature domains (e.g. UP: leftmost orientation domain, Down: rightmost orientation domain).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7

claim: Curvature preference domains generally progress from low to high curvature with distance across the cortex.
source: This reveals that the curvature preference domains generally progress from low to high curvature with distance across the cortex.
evidence: Supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 7D

claim: On average, across eight straight-to-curved sequences, there is a general trend of greater distance with increasing curvature.
source: However, on average (black line), across these eight straight-to-curved sequences, there is a general trend of greater distance with increasing curvature.
evidence: Supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 7D

claim: There are some domains with broad curvature preference.
source: However, there are some domains with broad curvature preference.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Curvature representation in V4 is complex.
source: This suggests the presence of a diversity in organization, indicating that curvature representation in V4 is complex.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing diversity

claim: Curvature domains do not co-localize with orientation pinwheel centers.
source: As shown in two cases in Figure 2—figure supplement 12 (Case 1: A-B, Case 2: C-D), the curvature domains (orange regions) do not co-localize with orientation pinwheel centers (blue dots).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 12

claim: Most of the pinwheel centers are outside the curvature domains entirely.
source: In fact, most of the pinwheel centers are outside the curvature domains entirely.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 12

claim: Pinwheel center responses to curvatures are weak and do not distinguish curvature from straight.
source: Moreover, as shown by the responses of pinwheel centers to straight and curved stimuli (Figure 2—figure supplement 12E), the pinwheel center responses to curvatures are weak and do not distinguish curvature from straight (Wilcoxon test, p=0.13).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: It is unlikely for pinwheel centers to be locations of curvature response.
source: This makes it unlikely for pinwheel centers to be locations of curvature response.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: Curvature responses are not simply a weighted sum of responses to component orientations.
source: We also considered the possibility that curvature responses are simply a weighted sum of responses to component orientations. This is unlikely because (1) the straight orientation domains are spatially distinct from the curvature domains (Figure 2). And (2) our analysis of response to component orientations compared with response to curvature shows that curvature domain response to straight component orientations is weak (smaller by roughly an order of magnitude) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by spatial analysis and response magnitude comparison

claim: End-stopped cells may contribute to curvature computation.
source: There is strong support for the role of end-stopped cells in curvature representation (Hubel and Wiesel, 1965; Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Dobbins et al., 1987; Sceniak et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: There is strong correlation between curvature preference and strength of end-stopping in V4.
source: Electrophysiological study of single unit responses to curvature gratings in V4 finds strong correlation between curvature preference and strength of end-stopping (Ponce et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: End-stopping, while an essential contributor to curvature computation, is not sufficient for all curvature encoding.
source: End-stopping, while an essential contributer to curvature computation, is not sufficient for all curvature encoding.
evidence: Inference from literature and current data

claim: Curvature selectivity displayed by many V4 neurons can be caused by complex structures of receptive field.
source: As supported by previous studies in V4 (Nandy et al., 2013; Nandy et al., 2016), the curvature selectivity displayed by many V4 neurons can also be caused by other properties (e.g. complex structures of receptive field).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Curvature domains are not equal to end-stopping domains.
source: While end-stopped cells may contribute to the curvature domain responses recorded here, curvature domains are not equal to end-stopping domains.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: End-stopping maps and curvature maps are distinct in V4.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 13, comparison of end-stopping maps (1 deg vs 4 deg straight gratings) and curvature maps reveal that they are distinct.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 13

claim: There are some regions of overlap (~33.3%) between end-stopping and curvature domains, but 66.7% of domains are in spatially distinct locations.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 13C (overlay of A, end-stopping map and B, curvature map) illustrates that there are some regions of overlap (~33.3%), but 66.7% of domains are in spatially distinct locations.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data

claim: Responses of curvature domains to straight stimuli are weaker than that to curved stimuli.
source: Moreover, quantification of curvature-preferring pixels (Figure 2—figure supplement 13D) reveals that, while there is a preference for the small over the large straight stimulus (compare two light gray lines), the responses to straight stimuli are still weaker than that to curved (black lines).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 13D

claim: In V4, curvature domains are not simply end-stopped domains.
source: This suggests that, in V4, curvature domains are not simply end-stopped domains.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: There is a systematic map of curvature representation in V4.
source: In summary, we provide evidence for the existence of curvature domains in V4 and show that there is a systematic map of curvature representation in V4.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Response preference for curvature is spatially mapped in certain parts of V4 from straight to highly curved.
source: The gradations of curvature degree across our stimulus set revealed that response preference is spatially mapped in certain parts of V4 (from straight to highly curved, Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,F

claim: Maps for curvature are distinct from those for straight orientation, color, high spatial frequency, orientation pinwheels, and end-stopping.
source: We showed that maps for curvature are distinct from those for straight orientation, color, high spatial frequency, orientation pinwheels, and end-stopping.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Curvature domains exhibit selectivity for degree of curvature (low to high), one which maps in a spatially shifting manner in V4.
source: We find curvature domains exhibit selectivity for degree of curvature (low to high), one which maps in a spatially shifting manner in V4.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Curvature degree progressions are not necessarily linear.
source: These progressions are not necessarily linear, as indicated by the distance changes related to curvature degree (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,H

claim: Similarity of response preference across both curved gratings and single curved lines provide evidence for curvature selectivity.
source: Similarity of response preference across both curved gratings and single curved lines provide further evidence for curvature selectivity rather than some other aspect of these stimuli.
evidence: Inference from experimental data using multiple stimulus types

claim: Straight and curved regions in V4 co-exist and occupy roughly complementary territory within the 'orientation bands' of V4.
source: We suggest that straight (large gray square) and curved (large gray oval) regions in V4 co-exist and occupy roughly complementary territory within the 'orientation bands' of V4.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings

claim: Within the curvature domains, there are multiple types of organizations, characterized by sequences of curvature degree as well as domains with complex curvature preference.
source: Within the curvature domains, there are multiple types of organizations, characterized by sequences of curvature degree as well as domains with complex curvature preference.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: No previous study has provided evidence suggesting that curvature is a basis for a hypercolumn in V4.
source: To our knowledge, no previous study has provided evidence suggesting that curvature is a basis for a hypercolumn in V4.
evidence: Statement of novelty based on literature knowledge

claim: Curvature domain responses are not due to a simple linear combination of local orientation domain responses.
source: Thus, it does not appear that curvature domain responses are due to a simple linear combination of local orientation domain responses, but result from a non-linear (perhaps multi-step) integration of straight oriented inputs.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: Curvature domain responses result from a non-linear integration of straight oriented inputs.
source: Thus, it does not appear that curvature domain responses are due to a simple linear combination of local orientation domain responses, but result from a non-linear (perhaps multi-step) integration of straight oriented inputs.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: Curvature domains and high spatial frequency maps in V4 differ.
source: High spatial frequency maps in V4 (first reported by Lu et al., 2018) differed from curvature maps (Figure 1H and L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation

claim: Less than 15% overall from three cases exhibited overlap between high spatial frequency domains and curvature domains.
source: On average, less than 15% overall from three cases exhibited overlap between high spatial frequency domains and curvature domains.

claim: Similar maps were obtained to gratings with different degrees of curvature.
source: Similar maps were obtained to gratings with different degrees of curvature (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Similar maps were obtained to gratings and single lines of the same curvature.
source: Similar maps were obtained to gratings and single lines of the same curvature (Figure 2K,L, Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K,L and Figure 6

claim: Maps obtained in response to scrambled curvature stimuli failed to produce curvature maps.
source: Maps obtained in response to scrambled curvature stimuli (which also contain high spatial frequencies but lack the structural curvature information) failed to produce curvature maps.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Curvature domains have little overlap with low spatial frequency domains.
source: Note also that these curvature domains have little overlap with low spatial frequency domains (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: A representation of curvature and spatial frequency content are distinct.
source: further indicating that a representation of curvature and spatial frequency content are distinct
evidence: Inference from experimental data

source: As previous studies suggested, size tuning or end stopping may play an important role in curvature detection (Hubel and Wiesel, 1965; Dobbins et al., 1987)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: End-stopping is not independent from curvature preference features.
source: and is not independent from curvature preference features (Ponce et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Neurons with complex receptive field structures may account for curvature preferences.
source: However, other studies have suggested neurons with complex receptive field structures may also account for curvature preferences (Nandy et al., 2013; Nandy et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: While end-stopping likely contributes to curvature response, there are also other relevant parameters contributing to curvature response.
source: For this reason, while end-stopping likely contributes to curvature response, there are also other relevant parameters contributing to curvature response.
evidence: Inference from literature and experimental data

claim: Surround suppressed and curvature domains are not the same.
source: Similar to previous studies (Ghose and Ts'o, 1997), we found there were size sensitive regions in V4 (Case 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 13A). However, while there was some overlap, the size sensitive regions were on the whole spatially distinct from the curvature domains (compare Figure 2—figure supplement 13A and B, overlay in C).

claim: Curvature preference response in V4 is not due to end-stopping alone.
source: Thus curvature preference response in V4 is not due to end-stopping alone.

claim: Curvature domains are a primary feature of V4 organization.
source: While the authors did not systematically explore the organization of curvature degree or curvature orientation, this elegant study further reinforces the concept that curvature domains are a primary feature of V4 organization.

claim: Three ~1–2 cm-sized curvature patches exist in the temporal lobe of macaque.
source: By conducting fMRI mapping in response to a large array of stimuli containing curved (rounded, spheres, faces) vs rectilinear (square shapes, pyramid arrays, buildings) objects, Yue et al., 2014 reported the presence of three ~ 1–2 cm-sized curvature patches in the temporal lobe of macaque.

claim: The region of V4 studied here corresponds well with Yue et al's PCP patch.
source: The region of V4 studied here corresponds well with Yue et al's PCP patch.
evidence: Inference from comparison with cited study

claim: 200–500 μm-sized curvature degree and curvature orientation domains exist within Yue's PCP patch.

claim: Little evidence for curvature response preference was found in V1.

claim: V1 is considered the 'orientation-emergent' area.

source: and V2 the 'cue-invariant orientation-emergent' area

source: we concur with the view that V4 is the 'curvature-emergent' area

source: Integration of signals from V4 curvature domains are likely to contribute to additional levels of systematic maps associated with lower (MCP, PFP) and higher (ACP, AFP) order object, face, and body patch representations (Bao et al., 2020).

claim: Higher level patches will contain systematic columnar maps.
source: We predict that these higher level patches will also contain systematic columnar maps.

claim: All procedures were performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guidelines and were approved by the Zhejiang University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All procedures were performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guidelines and were approved by the Zhejiang University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

source: Different a/b ratios were used (2, 5, see Figure 5B; 1, 4, 7, 10, see Figure 5C) to create different curvature degrees.

claim: Receptive field sizes of V4 neurons at the recording position are around 3–5 degrees.
source: As the receptive field sizes of V4 neurons at our recording position are around 3–5 degrees (Chen et al., 2014), our stimuli were set to 4° and presented monocularly during the experiment.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study
